props.title: The Princess and the Frog
props.initialSlug: Waitress kisses frog prince, magic turns her too

sections.content: The Princess and the Frog marked Disney's triumphant return to hand-drawn animation and their first Black princess. Set in 1920s New Orleans, the film reinvents the classic Grimm fairy tale with jazz-age flair and Creole culture. The movie's soundtrack by Randy Newman captures the era's jazz, zydeco, and blues, while the animation showcases the French Quarter's distinctive architecture and the mysterious bayou. Directors Ron Clements and John Musker, who helmed The Little Mermaid (1989) and Aladdin (1992), brought their signature mix of romance and comedy while breaking new ground with Tiana's entrepreneurial dreams.

sections.content: The film's themes of hard work versus "wishing on stars" represented a sharp departure from traditional Disney princess narratives. Unlike Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) or Sleeping Beauty (1959), Tiana's story emphasizes entrepreneurship and self-reliance. This shift reflects broader changes in animated storytelling, similar to the working-class dreams in An American Tail (1986) and the career ambitions in Mulan (1998).

The villain, Dr. Facilier, joins Disney's pantheon of memorable antagonists, with Keith David's mesmerizing performance and "Friends on the Other Side" standing alongside The Lion King's (1994) Scar and The Little Mermaid's (1989) Ursula. The film's exploration of voodoo and Louisiana folklore brings unique cultural elements rarely seen in mainstream animation, though handled with careful respect similar to the Polynesian mythology in Moana (2016). SUBHEAD: Cultural Impact and Animation Legacy

movies.title: Pocahontas
movies.slug: Disney's first attempt at incorporating American cultural history into their princess formula

sections.content: The Princess and the Frog influenced later Disney films' approach to cultural authenticity, paving the way for Brave (2012), Coco (2017), and Encanto (2021). The film's commercial performance, while solid, led Disney to pivot toward computer animation, making it one of the studio's last hand-drawn features alongside Winnie the Pooh (2011). However, its artistic achievement in traditional animation rivals classics like Bambi (1942) and Pinocchio (1940).
